questions.statement: Choose the correct past form of the verb "go": "Last Saturday, I _______ to the Flag Memorial (Monumento a la Bandera) in Rosario."
questions.context: Agustín le cuenta a su abuela sobre su fin de semana en Rosario.

options.text: goed
options.feedback: 'Go' is an irregular verb, so the past is not built by adding '-ed' to the base form.

options.text: went
options.feedback: Correct. 'Went' is the irregular past simple of 'go', and the sentence needs a single past-tense verb.

options.text: gone
options.feedback: 'Gone' is the past participle, which is used with an auxiliary such as 'have gone', not on its own in the past simple.

options.text: was go
options.feedback: The past simple does not use 'was' with the base form of the verb; that would be the passive or a progressive.

questions.explanation:
Para hablar de acciones terminadas en el pasado, usamos el pasado simple. Como "go" es un verbo irregular, tenés que memorizar que su pasado es "went". En Rosario, Agustín "went" al Monumento el sábado pasado.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence in Past Continuous: "At 5 PM yesterday, Valentina _______ a choripán in the park."
questions.context: Valentina describe lo que estaba haciendo ayer a la tarde en Córdoba.

options.text: were eating
options.feedback: 'Were' goes with plural subjects or 'you', but Valentina is 'she', so it takes 'was'.

options.text: was eating
options.feedback: Correct. The past continuous for 'she' is 'was' plus the verb in -ing, and 'at 5 PM yesterday' marks a moment in the past.

options.text: ate
options.feedback: 'Ate' is past simple and describes a finished action, not an action in progress at a specific past moment.

options.text: is eating
options.feedback: 'Is eating' is present continuous, but the sentence is set in the past with 'yesterday'.

questions.explanation:
El pasado continuo se usa para describir acciones que estaban ocurriendo en un momento puntual del pasado. Como Valentina es una sola persona (she), usamos "was" seguido del verbo con la terminación "-ing".

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly combines Past Simple and Past Continuous?
questions.context: Una charla sobre un corte de luz inesperado durante un partido de fútbol.

options.text: We were watching the Superclásico when the lights went out.
options.feedback: Correct. The past continuous gives the long background action that was under way ('we were watching') and the past simple gives the short interruption that cut it short ('the lights went out').

options.text: We watched the Superclásico when the lights were going out.
options.feedback: Here the longer background action 'we watched' is in past simple and the interruption 'were going out' is in past continuous, which reverses the usual roles.

options.text: We were watching the Superclásico when the lights were going out.
options.feedback: Using the continuous for both the watching and the interruption is unnatural; the short interruption belongs in past simple.

options.text: We watched the Superclásico when the lights went out.
options.feedback: This is grammatical but it loses the background: 'watched' in past simple does not show the match was already under way.

questions.explanation:
Es muy común usar estos dos tiempos juntos. El pasado continuo ("were watching") nos dice qué estábamos haciendo, y el pasado simple ("went out") nos cuenta qué interrumpió esa actividad. ¡Típico que se corte la luz justo en el medio del partido!

questions.statement: Fill in the blanks: "While I _______ (walk) down Florida Street, I _______ (see) a famous tango dancer."
questions.context: Un turista relata un pequeño incidente en la calle Florida, Buenos Aires.

options.text: walked / saw
options.feedback: 'While' introduces a long action already in progress, which takes the past continuous, not the past simple.

options.text: was walking / saw
options.feedback: Correct. Walking is the long background action in past continuous and seeing the dancer is the short interrupting action in past simple.

options.text: am walking / see
options.feedback: Both verbs are in the present, but the context is a past narrative.

options.text: was walking / was seeing
options.feedback: 'See' is a perception verb and is not normally used in the continuous in this sense.

questions.explanation:
La palabra "while" (mientras) es una pista clave: casi siempre va seguida del pasado continuo. Caminar por la calle Florida lleva tiempo ("was walking"), y el momento en que ves a alguien es instantáneo ("saw").

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct option: "I didn't answer your call because I _______ on the Subte and it _______ very noisy."
questions.context: Matías explica por qué no escuchó el teléfono mientras estaba en el subte.

options.text: traveled / was
options.feedback: Past simple 'traveled' does not convey what you were in the middle of doing at that moment; the continuous is more natural here.

options.text: was traveling / was
options.feedback: Correct. You were in the process of travelling, which takes 'was' plus -ing, and the state of the subway was noisy.

options.text: traveling / being
options.feedback: 'Traveling' and 'being' are missing the auxiliary verbs, so the sentence has no grammatical structure.

options.text: was travel / was
options.feedback: After 'was' the verb needs the -ing form; 'was travel' is not a form of the verb at all.

questions.explanation:
Matías está justificando una acción (no atender) con una situación que estaba en progreso (viajar en subte). Usamos "was traveling" para ese proceso. El verbo "to be" en pasado ("was") se usa para describir cómo era el ambiente.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: How do you ask what they were doing at a specific time? "What _______ when the storm started?"
questions.context: Una pregunta sobre las actividades de un grupo de amigos durante una tormenta en Mar del Plata.

options.text: they were doing
options.feedback: In a question the auxiliary 'were' has to come before the subject, not after it.

options.text: were they doing
options.feedback: Correct. The structure is word order plus 'were' plus subject plus verb-ing, giving 'were they doing'.

options.text: did they do
options.feedback: 'Did they do' would ask what they did at some point, not what they were in the middle of doing.

options.text: they did
options.feedback: 'They did' is missing the auxiliary for a past simple question and does not form the continuous at all.

questions.explanation:
Para preguntar sobre una acción en progreso en el pasado, invertimos el orden: Auxiliar (was/were) + Sujeto. Si querés saber qué hacían tus amigos en "La Feliz" cuando empezó a llover, preguntás "What were they doing?".

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: When two long actions happen simultaneously in the past, we can use Past Continuous for both. Which sentence is correct?
questions.context: Comparando dos acciones que ocurrieron al mismo tiempo en una oficina de Buenos Aires.

options.text: While Martina worked, Facundo was making coffee.
options.feedback: 'Worked' in past simple is understandable, but it is better to use the continuous for both actions to stress that two processes overlapped.

options.text: While Martina was working, Facundo was making coffee.
options.feedback: Correct. Both actions were in progress at the same time, which is exactly what past continuous for both expresses.

options.text: Martina was working while Facundo made coffee.
options.feedback: 'Made' in past simple cuts the idea of two long simultaneous processes.

options.text: Martina was work while Facundo was make coffee.
options.feedback: Both main verbs lack the -ing endings, so the continuous is not formed at all.

questions.explanation:
Si tenés dos personas haciendo cosas largas al mismo tiempo, podés usar el pasado continuo para las dos. Martina "was working" y Facundo "was making coffee". El "while" nos ayuda a conectar estas dos historias paralelas.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read the sentences and identify which action happened first: "When we arrived at the hotel, it was raining."
questions.context: Analizando el orden de los eventos en un viaje a la Quebrada de Humahuaca.

options.text: We arrived at the hotel first, and then it started to rain.
options.feedback: If the rain began after the arrival, past simple would be used instead: 'when we arrived at the hotel, it rained'.

options.text: It was already raining before we arrived.
options.feedback: Correct. The past continuous shows the rain was already going on as the background situation before the arrival.

options.text: Both actions started exactly at the same millisecond.
options.feedback: The wording is odd, and in any case the continuous clearly marks the rain as a situation that had already started.

options.text: The sentence is incorrect; you cannot use 'when' with Past Continuous.
options.feedback: There is nothing wrong with the sentence: 'when' is routinely used with a past continuous clause.

questions.explanation:
Este es un detalle sutil pero importante. Si usás el continuo ("it was raining"), estás diciendo que la lluvia ya estaba ahí cuando vos llegaste. El pasado continuo prepara el "escenario" de la historia.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that describes a sequence of completed actions (one after the other):
questions.context: Un relato sobre una pérdida de llaves en Mendoza.

options.text: I was looking for my keys when I found them in my pocket.
options.feedback: This describes a long action interrupted by a short one, not a list of steps completed one after the other.

options.text: I looked for my keys, found them in my pocket, and opened the door.
options.feedback: Correct. Past simple is used for a series of completed actions happening in successive order.

options.text: I was looking for my keys and finding them in my pocket.
options.feedback: It makes little sense to use the continuous for the precise moment of finding something.

options.text: While I looked for my keys, I was finding them.
options.feedback: This is awkward and it does not describe a logical sequence of finished events.

questions.explanation:
Cuando contás una historia paso a paso (primero esto, después aquello), usás siempre el pasado simple. Es como los goles de un partido: "pateó, atajó el arquero, dio en el palo". Cada acción está terminada antes de que empiece la siguiente.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which of these beginnings for a story creates a better "atmosphere"?
questions.context: Evaluación de la ambientación en el inicio de un cuento sobre la Patagonia.

options.text: The wind blew. The snow fell. We walked to the cabin.
options.feedback: It is grammatically correct, but it reads like a dry list of facts rather than creating atmosphere.

options.text: The wind was blowing and the snow was falling. We were walking slowly to the cabin.
options.feedback: Correct. Past continuous is ideal for setting the background or atmosphere of a scene, as it paints the ongoing situation rather than single completed events.

options.text: The wind blows and the snow falls. We walk to the cabin.
options.feedback: This is in the present tense, which moves the narration to a different time altogether.

options.text: The wind did blow and the snow did fall.
options.feedback: Using emphatic 'did' in an affirmative statement does not create background atmosphere.

questions.explanation:
En literatura, el pasado continuo es tu mejor amigo para las descripciones. Si querés que el lector se imagine el frío de la Patagonia, decís "the wind was blowing". Eso crea una imagen en movimiento en la mente del que lee.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: One of these sentences has a spelling error in the Past Continuous form. Identify it:
questions.context: Detectar un error común de "spelling" en los verbos con -ing en un examen.

options.text: We were traveling through the pampas. (British/International spelling)
options.feedback: This is correct; the double 'l' is standard in British and international spelling of 'travelling'.

options.text: They were sitting on the grass.
options.feedback: This is correct; the consonant is doubled in short one-syllable verbs ending in a single consonant, as in sit -> sitting.

options.text: She was writeing a letter to her cousin in Salta.
options.feedback: Correct. This one has the error: when a verb ends in a silent 'e', the 'e' is dropped before adding -ing, so 'write' becomes 'writing', not 'writeing'.

options.text: It was beginning to get dark.
options.feedback: This is correct; the 'n' is doubled because the final syllable is the stressed one, as in begin -> beginning.

questions.explanation:
¡Ojo al escribir! Si el verbo termina en "e" (como write, dance, smile), tenés que borrar esa "e" para poder agregar el "-ing". Entonces queda "writing". Es un error que muchos cometemos, ¡no te olvides!

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement:
Compare:
1. "I had a great time at the party in San Luis."
2. "I was having a great time when you called."
Is sentence 2 correct?
questions.context: Un desafío gramatical sobre verbos que cambian de significado entre Simple y Continuo.

options.text: Yes, because 'have a great time' is an experience/action, not just possession.
options.feedback: 'Have' as possession is a stative verb and does not go into the continuous, but 'have a great time' is an activity expression and can.

options.text: No, because 'have' is a stative verb and can never have -ing.
options.feedback: This is wrong: 'have' behaves differently depending on whether it means possession or is part of an activity phrase.

options.text: No, it should be "I had been having a great time".
options.feedback: 'I had been having a great time' is the past perfect continuous, which is far too complex and unnecessary here.

options.text: Yes, but only if the party is still happening now.
options.feedback: The phrase 'when you called' already marks the situation as past, so the party does not need to still be happening.

questions.explanation:
Esta es una regla avanzada. El verbo "have" no lleva -ing si hablás de tener algo (como una casa). Pero si lo usás en expresiones como "have a good time" o "have a shower", ahí sí funciona como una acción y podés usarlo en pasado continuo. ¡Muy bien si lo sacaste!
